items.stem: An organisation holds a current, unqualified audit report for a named security standard, then is breached the following week through an attack path the standard's scope never covered. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: Both can be true together: compliance is conformance to an external obligation over a past period, and security is whether the system actually resists attack.
options.why: The two properties are measured against different yardsticks, so neither state implies the other.

options.text: No, an organisation cannot be genuinely compliant while it remains breachable, because compliance implies the system was already secure against every attack.
options.why: This treats compliance as a claim about resisting attack, which is what the CIA triad measures, not what compliance measures.

options.text: No, a security standard's audit examines the CIA triad directly, so a clean report already means confidentiality, integrity and availability held against every possible attacker.
options.why: An audit examines evidence against the standard's own criteria and scope, not against every attack path the CIA triad might eventually face.

options.text: No, an unqualified report means the auditor found zero exceptions anywhere across the organisation's entire technology estate.
options.why: An unqualified report speaks only to the stated scope and period; it says nothing about systems the audit never examined.

items.rationale: Compliance is a claim about an organisation, measured against an obligation written outside the team that runs the system. Security is a claim about the system itself, tested against whether an attacker can defeat it. A system can satisfy one while failing the other, and the exam relies on candidates conflating the two.

items.stem: A team tells a new hire that their service is 'compliant' with an unnamed standard. What is missing before that claim means anything an auditor could actually test?

options.text: Which standard, over what period, and for what defined boundary the claim is being made.
options.why: Compliance is retrospective and scoped: compliance with something, over a period, for a boundary, and none of those has been named.

options.text: A written policy stating the organisation's intent to comply, signed off by leadership.
options.why: A policy states intent but sets no measurable threshold, so it cannot supply the missing standard, period or scope.

options.text: An inventory of the technical controls that are currently enabled across the service.
options.why: Naming controls is not the same as naming the standard, period and scope the compliance claim is measured against.

options.text: Nothing further, since 'compliant' is a complete claim once the organisation itself believes it to be true.
options.why: An auditor cannot test a belief; without the standard, period and scope, the claim has nothing to be checked against.

items.rationale: An organisation that says 'we are compliant' without naming the standard, the period and the scope has not said anything an auditor could test. The claim only becomes testable once all three are fixed.

items.stem: Which statement best distinguishes 'compliance' from 'security' as the exam uses the two terms?

options.text: Compliance is a claim about an organisation measured against an externally written obligation; security is a claim about a system measured against whether it resists attack.
options.why: This is the definitional split: who wrote the yardstick, and what it is measured against.

options.text: Compliance and the CIA triad are the same property, just reported in two different formats for two different audiences.
options.why: They are measured against different yardsticks: an external obligation versus the system's own confidentiality, integrity and availability.

options.text: Compliance is what an audit produces, and security is what a penetration test produces, so the two terms simply name different kinds of assessment report rather than two different properties.
options.why: This confuses the assessment method with the property assessed; an audit examines compliance evidence, but compliance is not defined by having been audited.

options.text: Compliance is the outcome of a completed risk assessment, and security is the outcome of choosing and implementing a risk response.
options.why: Risk assessment and risk response are activities within a broader security programme, not the definitions the exam draws for these two terms.

items.rationale: Compliance and security overlap heavily but are not the same claim. Compliance answers to a standard written outside the team; security answers to whether the system actually holds against attack. Recognising that a system can be fully one and not the other is the whole of the concept.

items.stem: An assessor writes a finding that a required control was not observed operating during the review period. Against which of policy, standard or procedure is that finding written, and why?

options.text: The standard, because it is the only tier that states a measurable, mandatory requirement, so it is the only one that can be failed on evidence.
options.why: Findings are written against standards precisely because a standard is the only tier with a testable threshold in it.

options.text: The procedure, because the finding concerns the exact steps that were, or were not, followed by staff to satisfy the requirement on the day in question.
options.why: A procedure gives the steps that satisfy a standard; the failure itself is written against the standard the steps were supposed to meet.

options.text: The policy, because it states the organisation's overall intent to have the control in place at all.
options.why: A policy alone cannot be failed on evidence; it has no threshold, so an assessor has nothing to test it against.

options.text: A guideline, since guidelines are the tier auditors check first before moving on to mandatory requirements.
options.why: A guideline is recommended, not mandatory, so it carries nothing an assessor could fail; that is exactly why it is the usual distractor here.

items.rationale: Policy states intent, a standard sets a measurable and mandatory requirement, and a procedure gives the steps that satisfy the standard. Findings are written against standards because that is the only tier with something testable in it.

items.stem: A team rewrites its incident-response runbook to reflect a newly adopted ticketing tool, with no other change to what is required or expected. Which tier changed, and what does that imply for the compliance boundary?

options.text: The procedure changed; that is routine operational work and does not by itself move what an assessor tests against.
options.why: Rewriting a procedure is routine operational work, unlike changing a standard, which moves the compliance boundary.

options.text: The standard changed, so the compliance boundary has moved and the change needs management sign-off before it takes effect.
options.why: Nothing about the measurable requirement changed here, only the steps used to satisfy it, so the standard was never touched.

options.text: The policy changed, so the organisation's stated intent and who is bound by it has shifted as a result.
options.why: A policy states intent and who is bound; swapping the ticketing tool changes neither.

options.text: Nothing changed at any tier, because a runbook sits entirely outside the policy, standard and procedure hierarchy.
options.why: A runbook is exactly the procedure tier, the steps that satisfy a standard, so it is not outside the hierarchy at all.

items.rationale: The three tiers change at different costs and by different authority. A procedure is routine operational work to update; a standard changes what an assessor tests against, so changing it moves the compliance boundary and typically needs sign-off.

items.stem: A team enables multi-factor authentication on every externally reachable SSH endpoint and can show the configuration export to prove it. An assessor asks for something more before crediting the control. What is missing?

options.text: Evidence that the control actually challenged users during the audit period, such as the authentication logs, not just the configuration showing it is turned on.
options.why: A configuration export is evidence of design; the logs for the period are the evidence that the control operated.

options.text: A completed audit report that lists multi-factor authentication as being within its examined scope.
options.why: An audit is a periodic examination of evidence by an assessor; it is not itself the evidence the control produced day to day.

options.text: A written policy that requires multi-factor authentication on all externally reachable endpoints.
options.why: A policy document is evidence a control was designed, never evidence that it actually operated.

options.text: Nothing further; the enabled setting shown in the configuration export is itself sufficient proof that the control actually ran and challenged users throughout the entire audit period.
options.why: 'We have it enabled' is an assurance, not evidence; only the logs proving it actually challenged users during the period count as evidence.

items.rationale: A control is the safeguard; evidence is the artifact showing it operated. A configuration export shows the control was designed. Only logs, tickets or review records generated as a by-product of the control running during the period count as evidence that it operated.

items.stem: A file-integrity monitor alerts the security team within minutes whenever a production binary changes unexpectedly, but does not itself block the change or revert it. How is that control classified by function?

options.text: Detective, because it notices that a change happened rather than stopping it beforehand or restoring the system afterward.
options.why: File integrity checking and log monitoring are the guide's own examples of detective controls.

options.text: Preventive, because the alert is generated early enough to stop the unauthorised change before it takes full effect.
options.why: The monitor reports after the change has already occurred; nothing described blocks it from happening.

options.text: Corrective, because the security team's response to the alert restores the binary to a known-good state before any further damage can occur.
options.why: The scenario describes only the alert itself; nothing about the monitor performs the restoration that would make it corrective.

options.text: Administrative, because responding to the alert is a documented process the security team follows by hand.
options.why: The monitor itself is a technical mechanism enforced by the system, not a documented human process.

items.rationale: Controls are classified by function as preventive, detective or corrective, and by nature as administrative, technical or physical. A monitor that notices and reports a change without blocking or reversing it is a technical, detective control.

items.stem: An assessor reviews 25 of the 400 access-approval tickets generated during the audit period and finds all 25 correctly authorised. What can the assessor conclude from that review alone?

options.text: That the sampled tickets support the control having operated correctly for the period tested, not that every one of the 400 tickets was individually checked.
options.why: An assessor samples items from the period and checks each one rather than examining the entire population.

options.text: That all 400 tickets were reviewed, since a clean sample of this size statistically implies the whole population of tickets must also be clean.
options.why: Sampling explicitly does not examine everything; the assessor's conclusion only covers the items actually sampled.

options.text: That the organisation is now compliant with the relevant standard permanently, since the audit examining this control is finished.
options.why: An audit's opinion covers a fixed scope and period; it is not a permanent state and does not extend indefinitely into the future.

options.text: That the approval control is preventive rather than detective, since the tickets show approval happened before access was granted.
options.why: Whether approval happens before or after access is a design question about the control's function, not something this sample review establishes.

items.rationale: An assessor examines evidence by sampling rather than by checking every item the control produced. A clean sample supports, but does not prove, that the control operated correctly across the full population for the tested period.

items.stem: A vendor answers a due-diligence request by saying 'we have multi-factor authentication enabled, and a written policy requiring it.' What is still missing before an assessor can credit the control as audited?

options.text: Evidence the control actually operated during the stated period; an audit examines evidence, not assurances or documented intent.
options.why: Audits examine evidence, not assurances, and neither an enabled setting nor a policy is evidence of operation.

options.text: Nothing further; the enabled setting plus the written policy together are exactly what counts as evidence of a control operating.
options.why: A policy document is evidence a control was designed, never evidence it operated; that gap is exactly what audits exist to catch.

options.text: A signed statement from the vendor's chief executive personally attesting that the control works as described.
options.why: An executive attestation is an assurance, not the sampled artifact an assessor actually examines.

options.text: Confirmation of whether the control is classified as preventive rather than detective in the vendor's own internal control catalogue and taxonomy.
options.why: Classifying the control's function settles nothing about whether it actually produced evidence of operating during the period.

items.rationale: An audit is a formal examination of evidence against defined criteria, within a scope and period. Neither a configuration setting nor a policy document is evidence that a control operated; only artifacts generated by the control running during the period qualify.

items.stem: A prospective customer asks whether a vendor's controls were merely designed correctly, or actually operated correctly, over the last six months. Which report answers that question, and why?

options.text: A Type 2 report, because it tests operating effectiveness across a period, while a Type 1 report addresses design as of a single date.
options.why: A point-in-time examination asks whether controls were suitably designed; a period examination asks whether they operated effectively.

options.text: A Type 1 report, since confirming the design of a control already implies it was exercised correctly afterward.
options.why: A Type 1 report addresses design as of one date; it makes no claim about how the control performed in the months that followed.

options.text: Either report equally, since both examine exactly the same underlying evidence and only differ in how the findings happen to be formatted.
options.why: The two report shapes are routinely confused, but a point-in-time design opinion and a period operating-effectiveness opinion rest on different amounts of evidence.

options.text: An ISO 27001 certificate, since certification always speaks to a rolling period of operation rather than a single date.
options.why: ISO 27001 issues certification through an accredited body, a different artifact entirely from either SOC 2 report shape being asked about here.

items.rationale: A SOC 2 Type 1 report asks whether controls were suitably designed on a given date; a Type 2 report asks whether they operated effectively across months. The second costs more to obtain and claims more about the intervening period.

items.stem: A company's own internal security team reviews its access controls and issues a clean internal report. What can the company now claim to an outside party asking for independent assurance?

options.text: That an internal review found no exceptions, not that an independent assessor has examined anything.
options.why: An audit can be internal or performed by an independent external assessor, and the two carry different standing.

options.text: That it is now audited in exactly the sense a customer's due-diligence questionnaire is asking about.
options.why: Being un-audited by an independent party is not the same as non-compliant, but a clean internal review is also not the same as an independent audit result.

options.text: That every control it operates now has documented evidence, since conducting the review process itself creates that evidence.
options.why: The review is the examination; whether the controls it examined already had evidence produced is a separate, prior question the review does not settle.

options.text: That the company holds a certification, since a clean internal report and an accredited certification carry the same standing.
options.why: Certification is issued by an accredited external body; an internal review, however clean, is not that.

items.rationale: An audit can be internal, the organisation examining itself, or performed by an independent external assessor. The two are not interchangeable claims, and a clean internal review does not license a claim of independent assurance.

items.stem: A team finishes ranking its risks by likelihood and impact, but has not yet decided what to do about any of them. What has the team completed, and what still remains?

options.text: The risk assessment is complete; choosing to accept, avoid, mitigate, share or transfer each risk, the risk response, still remains.
options.why: Deciding what to do about a risk is a separate activity, risk response, that follows the assessment.

options.text: Both the assessment and the response are complete, since ranking the risks by likelihood and impact already implies a decision about how to handle each one.
options.why: Ranking risks by likelihood and impact says nothing about which response, if any, has been chosen for each of them.

options.text: An audit is complete, and the risk assessment itself still remains to be carried out.
options.why: Nothing in the scenario involves an assessor examining evidence against criteria; this is risk identification and ranking, not an audit.

options.text: A compliance obligation is now satisfied, and only paperwork documenting the ranking remains.
options.why: A risk assessment is an internal activity and does not by itself satisfy any external compliance obligation.

items.rationale: Risk assessment identifies risks and estimates likelihood and impact so they can be prioritised. Deciding what to do about each one, accept, avoid, mitigate, share or transfer, is risk response, a distinct activity that follows the assessment.

items.stem: A start-up ranks credential theft as its top risk during a review, then buys cyber-insurance covering breach-related costs. What has it just done?

options.text: Chosen a risk response, specifically transfer, which is a legitimate outcome distinct from the assessment that identified the risk.
options.why: Buying insurance transfers the financial consequence of the risk to a third party, one of the named risk responses.

options.text: Mitigated the risk, since holding insurance reduces the likelihood that credential theft will actually occur.
options.why: Insurance changes who bears the cost of an incident; it does not reduce the likelihood of the incident happening, which is what mitigation targets.

options.text: Nothing meaningful from a risk standpoint, since insurance is purely a financial product rather than a recognised risk response in its own right.
options.why: Transfer, alongside accept, avoid, mitigate and share, is one of the named risk responses, and insurance is a standard example of it.

options.text: Completed a fresh risk assessment, since buying insurance re-ranks the likelihood and impact of the underlying risk.
options.why: Purchasing insurance is a response to a risk that was already ranked, not a re-run of the identification and ranking activity.

items.rationale: Risk response is the separate activity of deciding what to do about an already-assessed risk. Accepting, avoiding, mitigating, sharing and transferring are the five recognised responses, and buying insurance is a textbook case of transfer.

items.stem: A US-only retailer with no establishment anywhere in the EU sells directly to consumers who are physically located in Germany and France. Does GDPR reach that retailer, and on what basis?

options.text: Yes, under Article 3(2): a controller with no EU establishment is still reached when it offers goods or services to data subjects who are in the Union.
options.why: Article 3(2) extends GDPR to a non-established controller offering goods or services to, or monitoring, people who are in the Union.

options.text: No, GDPR only binds companies with an establishment somewhere inside the EU, so a US-only retailer sits outside its scope regardless of where its customers happen to be.
options.why: Article 3(2) reaches a non-established controller or processor exactly when it offers goods or services to, or monitors, people in the Union.

options.text: No, GDPR, like PCI-DSS, only binds an organisation through a contract it has signed, and this retailer has signed nothing with any EU regulator.
options.why: GDPR is a directly applicable law with statutory territorial reach; PCI-DSS is the contractual regime, and conflating the two mischaracterises GDPR's basis for reaching this retailer.

options.text: Yes, because the customers involved are citizens of European Union member states.
options.why: GDPR's territorial test in Article 3 turns on where the data subject is, not on their citizenship, a distinction the exam tests directly.

items.rationale: Article 3 gives GDPR extraterritorial reach through two limbs: 3(1) turns on an EU establishment's activities, and 3(2) reaches a non-established controller or processor offering goods or services to, or monitoring, people who are in the Union. Citizenship is not a condition in either limb.

items.stem: A controller becomes aware of a personal data breach at 09:00 on Monday. It assesses the breach as unlikely to create a high risk to the affected individuals, though some risk to their rights and freedoms remains. What is required of the controller by Wednesday at 09:00?

options.text: Notification to the competent supervisory authority, without undue delay and, where feasible, within the 72-hour window.
options.why: Article 33 requires notifying the supervisory authority within 72 hours where feasible, unless the breach is unlikely to result in any risk to rights and freedoms.

options.text: Notification to every individual affected by the breach, since any residual risk at all triggers the individual-notification duty.
options.why: Individual notification is triggered only by a likely high risk to the individuals, which the scenario says has not been assessed as present.

options.text: Nothing, since the breach was assessed as unlikely to cause a high risk to the affected individuals.
options.why: The 72-hour authority-notification duty is excused only when the breach is unlikely to result in any risk to rights and freedoms, and some risk remains here.

options.text: A report to an Approved Scanning Vendor documenting the scope of the exposure.
options.why: An Approved Scanning Vendor is a role tied to external vulnerability scanning under PCI-DSS and has no part in GDPR's breach-notification duty.

items.rationale: Article 33 fixes a 72-hour clock, where feasible, for notifying the supervisory authority of a breach, excused only when the breach is unlikely to result in any risk to rights and freedoms. Notifying affected individuals is a separate duty with no fixed hour count, triggered only by a likely high risk to them.

items.stem: A company hosts its EU customer database in a Frankfurt data centre and tells its auditors this permanently settles GDPR's rules on where the data may go. What has it overlooked?

options.text: That EU residency is not a general requirement GDPR imposes; the rules restrict transfers to third countries, and a lawful transfer mechanism still permits the data to leave later.
options.why: GDPR imposes no general localisation rule; Chapter V restricts third-country transfers rather than forbidding them outright.

options.text: Nothing; GDPR requires that personal data physically remain within the European Union at all times once collected.
options.why: GDPR contains no general data-localisation rule; Chapter V governs conditions for transferring data out, not a blanket requirement to keep it in.

options.text: That hosting location is irrelevant, since GDPR, like PCI-DSS, is really just a contractual standard rather than a statute and never itself governs where data may be kept.
options.why: GDPR is a directly applicable regulation, a statute, not a contractual standard, and conflating the two mischaracterises both frameworks.

options.text: That residency and sovereignty are the same fact, so choosing an EU region also fixes which legal system ultimately governs the data.
options.why: Residency is where data physically sits; sovereignty also depends on whose law the hosting operator itself answers to, which an EU region alone does not settle.

items.rationale: GDPR's Chapter V restricts transferring personal data to third countries through an adequacy decision, appropriate safeguards, or a specific derogation. It does not require data to stay in the EU, so a lawful transfer mechanism still allows the data to leave.

items.stem: A consumer fitness app collects heart-rate data directly from its users and is not affiliated with any hospital, insurer, clearinghouse or health-care provider. Does HIPAA govern that data?

options.text: No, HIPAA's scope follows who holds the data, and an app that is neither a covered entity nor a business associate falls outside it, however sensitive the data is.
options.why: HIPAA's scope is defined by who holds the data, not by how sensitive it is.

options.text: Yes, because health data as sensitive as a heart-rate reading is automatically protected health information under HIPAA wherever it happens to be collected or held.
options.why: The same reading is protected health information inside a hospital's system and outside HIPAA entirely in an unaffiliated consumer app; sensitivity alone does not trigger coverage.

options.text: Yes, because GDPR treats health data as a special category and HIPAA extends the same special-category classification to US-based apps.
options.why: HIPAA's coverage test turns on the entity's role as a covered entity or business associate, not on a special-category classification imported from a different law.

options.text: Only if the app keeps the data for longer than the retention period HIPAA mandates for consumer health apps.
options.why: Retention period has no bearing on whether HIPAA applies in the first place; applicability turns on the entity's role, which the scenario has already ruled out.

items.rationale: HIPAA binds covered entities, health plans, clearinghouses, and providers transmitting health information electronically, plus their business associates. An app collecting the same kind of data outside that relationship is simply not in scope, regardless of sensitivity.

items.stem: An implementation specification under the HIPAA Security Rule is marked 'addressable.' A team decides the specification is not reasonable for its environment and stops there, doing nothing further. Have they met the requirement?

options.text: No, they must also document why it is not a reasonable and appropriate safeguard and implement an equivalent alternative measure where one is reasonable and appropriate.
options.why: Addressable requires an assessment plus either implementation or a documented alternative, not merely a decision to skip it.

options.text: Yes, 'addressable' means the entity may choose to skip the specification entirely at its own discretion, with no further obligation to assess or document anything.
options.why: Addressable does not mean optional; the entity must still assess it and act, either by implementing it or by documenting an equivalent alternative.

options.text: Yes, only specifications labelled 'required' carry any obligation at all, so an addressable one imposes nothing further once the team has assessed it and moved on.
options.why: Addressable specifications still carry an obligation, to assess and then either implement or document an alternative, just not a fixed mandate to implement exactly as written.

options.text: No, but only because they must instead notify affected individuals within 60 days of making that decision.
options.why: The 60-day clock in the guide governs breach notification to affected individuals, not how an addressable specification decision is handled.

items.rationale: An addressable implementation specification requires the entity to assess whether it is reasonable and appropriate in its environment, implement it if so, and otherwise document why not and implement an equivalent alternative measure if one is reasonable and appropriate.

items.stem: A payment processor stores the card verification code printed on the back of customer cards, encrypted, for six months after each transaction completes, in case of later disputes. Is that consistent with PCI-DSS?

options.text: No, sensitive authentication data such as the card verification code may not be retained after authorisation, even encrypted, outside the narrow issuer carve-out.
options.why: The prohibition on retaining sensitive authentication data after authorisation applies regardless of encryption, with an exception only for issuers and issuing-support companies.

options.text: Yes, because encrypting the data satisfies any PCI-DSS restriction on storage, regardless of what category of card data is actually being stored or for how long.
options.why: Encryption does not create an exception; sensitive authentication data may not be retained after authorisation whether or not it is encrypted.

options.text: Yes, provided the processor can point to a documented lawful basis for the retention under Article 6.
options.why: A GDPR lawful basis governs personal-data processing under EU law; it does not create an exception to PCI-DSS's separate, contractual prohibition on retaining sensitive authentication data.

options.text: No, but only because six months exceeds the retention period set out in the processor's own internal policy.
options.why: The prohibition here is absolute for sensitive authentication data after authorisation; it does not turn on the length of any policy the processor might set for itself.

items.rationale: PCI-DSS's data rules run in opposite directions for different categories of card data. Sensitive authentication data, including the verification code, must not be stored after authorisation even if encrypted, with the exception reserved for issuers and issuing-support companies with a documented business need.

items.stem: A merchant stores the primary account number for recurring billing, rendered unreadable everywhere it sits, and retains no card verification code at all. Is the merchant meeting PCI-DSS's data-storage expectations, and who could ultimately withdraw its ability to accept cards over a violation?

options.text: Yes on storage; the account number may be retained if rendered unreadable, and correctly no verification code is kept, and a violation is enforced through the payment brands and acquirer, not a government regulator.
options.why: The account number may be stored if rendered unreadable, unlike sensitive authentication data, and enforcement runs through the merchant agreement.

options.text: Yes on storage, and violations are enforced by a government regulator empowered under card-industry legislation.
options.why: PCI-DSS is not legislation; the Council states that requiring or validating compliance is at the discretion of the payment brands and acquirers, not a statutory regulator.

options.text: No, storing the primary account number at all breaches PCI-DSS regardless of how it is rendered unreadable, in exactly the same way that GDPR restricts transferring personal data outside the European Union to third countries.
options.why: The primary account number may be stored if rendered unreadable; the guide's contrast with GDPR's transfer rules does not extend to forbidding account-number storage outright.

options.text: Yes on storage, and enforcement for a violation runs through the supervisory authority in the merchant's home country.
options.why: PCI-DSS has no supervisory authority of its own; that mechanism belongs to statutory regimes such as GDPR, not to a card-industry contract.

items.rationale: PCI-DSS permits the primary account number to be stored if rendered unreadable, while sensitive authentication data may not be retained after authorisation at all. It is contractual, not governmental, and is enforced through the merchant agreement with an acquirer and the payment brands rather than by a regulator.

items.stem: Which statement correctly describes how PCI-DSS binds an organisation that stores, processes or transmits cardholder data?

options.text: Through a contract, specifically the merchant agreement with an acquiring bank and the payment brands' own compliance programs, not through legislation.
options.why: PCI-DSS is contractual, not governmental, unlike GDPR and HIPAA.

options.text: Through statute, since handling payment card data is regulated the same way processing personal data is regulated under GDPR.
options.why: PCI-DSS is contractual, not governmental; a distractor calling it a regulation or a law is wrong for exactly that reason.

options.text: Through the same extraterritorial statutory mechanism as GDPR's Article 3, reaching any entity anywhere in the world that ever touches card data at all.
options.why: Article 3 is GDPR's statutory scope test; PCI-DSS reaches an organisation through a signed merchant agreement, not through legislation with territorial reach.

options.text: Through certification by an accredited body, the same mechanism ISO 27001 uses to bind organisations to its requirements.
options.why: ISO 27001 certification is issued by an accredited body; PCI-DSS validation instead runs through self-assessment or a Qualified Security Assessor under the acquirer's and brands' programs.

items.rationale: PCI-DSS is published by the PCI Security Standards Council and covers anyone storing, processing or transmitting cardholder data, but it is not legislation. Whether it must be complied with, and how, is set by the payment brands and acquirers through the merchant agreement.

items.stem: A vendor tells a customer it is 'SOC 2 certified.' What is wrong with that claim, and how does it differ from what ISO 27001 actually provides?

options.text: SOC 2 produces an examination report from a CPA firm, never a certificate; ISO 27001 is the one of the two that produces certification, through an accredited body.
options.why: SOC 2 yields a report, Type 1 on design or Type 2 on operation, while ISO 27001 certifies an information security management system.

options.text: Nothing is wrong; SOC 2 and ISO 27001 both issue certificates, just from different kinds of assessor.
options.why: SOC 2 yields a report, not a certificate; treating the two frameworks' outputs as interchangeable is exactly the wrong-sounding-right distractor the term invites.

options.text: Nothing is wrong; SOC 2 is a statutory requirement for any organisation that processes customer data of any kind whatsoever.
options.why: SOC 2 is a voluntary AICPA attestation framework, not a law, and it does not require anything of organisations that never choose to adopt it.

options.text: The claim is wrong because SOC 2 is actually a card-industry standard rather than a voluntary security attestation framework adopted by choice.
options.why: SOC 2 is an AICPA framework covering security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality or privacy, and has nothing to do with card payments.

items.rationale: SOC 2 and ISO 27001 are both voluntary frameworks organisations adopt to evidence their security posture, but neither is a law and their outputs differ: SOC 2 produces an examination report, never a certificate, while ISO 27001 produces certification through an accredited body.

items.stem: A company selects a cloud region in Ireland to host its EU customer data and considers the question of where the data's legal system sits fully settled. What has it actually settled?

options.text: Residency, where the data physically sits, but not necessarily sovereignty, which also depends on whose law the operator itself answers to.
options.why: A provider incorporated elsewhere may remain subject to its home jurisdiction's demands regardless of where the bytes live.

options.text: Both residency and sovereignty; choosing an EU region automatically resolves which legal system governs the data.
options.why: Sovereignty follows from residency and from who operates the service and under whose law that operator is incorporated, not from region choice alone.

options.text: Neither, since GDPR requires a specific derogation before any EU region may lawfully be used to host personal data belonging to residents at all.
options.why: GDPR imposes no general localisation rule and needs no derogation for data that simply stays within the EU; derogations concern transfers to third countries instead.

options.text: Retention, since choosing a region also fixes how long the data may lawfully be kept.
options.why: Region choice has no bearing on retention periods, which are set by separate statutory, contractual or purpose-based rules.

items.rationale: Residency is where data physically sits; sovereignty is which legal system it is subject to, following from residency and from who operates the service and under whose law. Selecting an EU region fixes residency but does not, on its own, settle sovereignty.

items.stem: A US-incorporated cloud provider hosts a customer's data in its Frankfurt region. A US law-enforcement request compels the provider to produce that data. What does this illustrate?

options.text: That sovereignty follows the operator's own legal exposure as well as the data's physical location, so an EU region does not by itself put the data outside the reach of the provider's home jurisdiction.
options.why: A provider's home-jurisdiction obligations can follow it regardless of where the data physically resides.

options.text: That the request is automatically unlawful, since data stored anywhere inside the EU is always completely outside the reach of any non-EU jurisdiction's law-enforcement demands, however framed.
options.why: Residency alone does not determine which legal systems can reach the data; a provider's home-jurisdiction obligations can follow it regardless of region.

options.text: That the provider has breached GDPR's transfer rules merely by receiving the request.
options.why: Chapter V governs transferring data out of the EU, not a third-party jurisdiction's request directed at the operator; whether an actual transfer under Chapter V has occurred is a separate question.

options.text: That the customer's contract with the provider determines sovereignty regardless of incorporation or hosting location.
options.why: A contract can allocate responsibilities between the parties, but it cannot change which legal system has authority to compel the operator that answers to it.

items.rationale: Sovereignty depends on residency and on whose law the operator itself is subject to. A provider incorporated in one jurisdiction can remain answerable to that jurisdiction's lawful demands even when the data it holds physically sits elsewhere.

items.stem: A payroll system retains statutory tax records for the legally required period, and a former employee submits a GDPR erasure request covering those same records. How is this resolved?

options.text: Neither rule wins outright: Article 17(3) disapplies erasure to the extent processing is necessary for a legal retention obligation, so the covered records are kept and everything outside that carve-out is erased.
options.why: GDPR resolves the conflict explicitly, carving out only the specific records the retention obligation covers.

options.text: The erasure request must be honoured in full immediately, since GDPR's erasure right overrides any other obligation the organisation may have.
options.why: Article 17(3) explicitly disapplies erasure to the extent a legal retention obligation requires the processing, so a blanket erasure would itself be non-compliant.

options.text: The records must be destroyed immediately once the employee's last working day arrives, since the organisation's own retention-and-disposal practice requires deleting data as soon as its purpose has ended for good.
options.why: That practice governs the organisation's own ceiling on keeping data once its purpose ends; a statutory retention obligation is a floor imposed from outside that this practice must still respect.

options.text: The retention obligation is void because the organisation's own internal policy states that data should be deleted once it is no longer actively used.
options.why: An obligation imposed from outside the organisation cannot be shortened by an internal policy that disagrees with it.

items.rationale: Data retention obligations are floors imposed from outside, pointing in the opposite direction from an erasure right. GDPR Article 17(3) reconciles the two explicitly, disapplying erasure only to the extent a legal obligation requires the processing, so the two rules are reconciled record category by record category rather than one simply overriding the other.

items.stem: Litigation becomes reasonably anticipated over a dataset that is simultaneously past its retention schedule's maximum and the subject of an active GDPR erasure request. What governs the data now?

options.text: A legal hold, which overrides both the retention schedule and the erasure request, freezing the data in place until the hold is released.
options.why: Once litigation or an investigation is anticipated, a legal hold preserves the relevant data ahead of both the schedule and any erasure request.

options.text: The erasure request, since a data subject's rights take precedence over any internal concern about pending litigation.
options.why: A legal hold is described as overriding both the schedule and an erasure request once litigation becomes anticipated, exactly the situation described here.

options.text: The retention schedule's maximum, since it was reached first and nothing can extend a schedule once its ceiling has arrived.
options.why: A legal hold specifically overrides the schedule's maximum once litigation becomes anticipated, which is exactly what has happened in this scenario.

options.text: The Clear, Purge or Destroy disposal framework, since the data is now past its maximum and due for sanitisation.
options.why: A disposal framework applies once data is actually being disposed of; a legal hold means disposal is paused, not proceeding, until it is released.

items.rationale: A legal hold freezes data in place once litigation or an investigation is reasonably anticipated, overriding both the retention schedule's normal maximum and any pending erasure request, until the hold itself is released.

items.stem: A team deletes a customer's row from its primary database in response to an erasure request, but the same data still exists unmodified in nightly backups and an analytics warehouse. Has disposal actually occurred?

options.text: No, the same data held in backups, archives and analytics copies is governed by the same schedule, and disposal means verified, documented destruction of every copy.
options.why: NIST SP 800-88 frames disposal as verified and documented, and backups and other copies are the same data under the same schedule.

options.text: Yes, deleting the row in the primary database is exactly what 'we deleted the record' is generally understood to mean.
options.why: 'We deleted the record' usually means one row in one database, while backups, archives and analytics copies remain the same data under the same schedule.

options.text: Yes, provided the primary-database deletion is logged as evidence for a future audit to examine.
options.why: A log entry evidences that one action took place; it does not establish that every remaining copy of the data was actually destroyed.

options.text: No, but only because the analytics warehouse falls entirely outside GDPR's definition of processing personal data.
options.why: Analytics copies of personal data are processing like any other; the actual gap here is that they were never disposed of, not that they fall outside scope.

items.rationale: Disposal is verified, documented destruction of every copy of the data, not deletion of a single pointer in one system. Backups, archives, log aggregators and analytics copies hold the same data and are governed by the same retention schedule.

items.stem: A checkout form has a marketing-communications box pre-ticked by default, and a user completes the purchase without unticking it. Under GDPR Article 6, has the user given a valid lawful basis for that marketing processing by consent?

options.text: No, valid consent must be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous, and a pre-ticked box or silence does not meet that bar.
options.why: A pre-ticked box or silence is not an unambiguous affirmative action, so it does not amount to valid consent.

options.text: Yes, completing the purchase without going back to untick the box is itself an unambiguous affirmative action indicating clear agreement.
options.why: A pre-ticked box or silence is explicitly not an unambiguous affirmative action, so no valid consent was given here.

options.text: Yes, because contract is one of the six lawful bases and this processing occurred during a contractual transaction.
options.why: Marketing communications are not necessary to perform the purchase contract, so contract cannot supply the lawful basis for them, and the question is specifically about consent.

options.text: No, but only because the checkout form failed to name a supervisory authority the user could contact.
options.why: Naming a supervisory authority has nothing to do with whether consent was validly obtained; the defect here is the pre-ticked box itself.

items.rationale: GDPR Article 6(1) lists six lawful bases, of which consent is only one. Valid consent must be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous; a pre-ticked box or silence is neither, so no lawful basis has been established by consent here.

items.stem: A company modifies a GPLv3-licensed program and runs the modified version only as an internal backend service that its own employees use, never distributing a copy of it to anyone outside the company. Does the GPL's source-disclosure duty apply?

options.text: No, GPLv3's trigger is conveying a copy, and running the software as an internal-only service transfers no copy to anyone outside the organisation.
options.why: GPLv3 states that mere interaction with a user through a computer network, with no transfer of a copy, is not conveying.

options.text: Yes, because 'free' software always requires publishing any modifications regardless of how the program ends up being used.
options.why: Open source removes the fee, not the licence's specific conditions; GPLv3's disclosure duty is triggered by conveying, which internal-only use does not do.

options.text: Yes, because the AGPL requires offering source to any user interacting remotely with a modified version, and that licence controls here.
options.why: The scenario names GPLv3, not the AGPL, and even under the AGPL the trigger is remote interaction by outside users, not merely internal employee use.

options.text: No, but only because the company has not yet exceeded a licensed per-seat entitlement for the software.
options.why: Per-seat entitlements are a proprietary-licensing concept; GPLv3's obligations turn on conveying a copy, not on how many seats are in use.

items.rationale: Copyleft licences such as the GPL trigger their source-disclosure duty on conveying, not on mere use. GPLv3 states outright that interacting with a user over a network without transferring a copy is not conveying, so running a modified version purely as an internal service does not by itself require publishing source.

items.stem: A team ships a product that bundles an MIT-licensed library but strips the library's copyright and permission notice out of the redistributed copy. Which obligation has been broken?

options.text: MIT's sole condition, that the copyright notice and the permission notice be included in all copies or substantial portions of the software.
options.why: MIT's entire condition is that these notices travel with the code in every copy or substantial portion distributed.

options.text: None, since MIT-licensed code carries no conditions at all once it has been redistributed to anyone else.
options.why: MIT is permissive, not condition-free; its whole condition is that the copyright and permission notices travel with the code.

options.text: The GPL's copyleft requirement to make corresponding source available to recipients of the distributed derivative.
options.why: The library here is MIT-licensed, a permissive licence with no copyleft source-provision duty; that obligation belongs to licences such as the GPL.

options.text: Apache 2.0's requirement to mark any changed file with a prominent notice stating that it was modified.
options.why: The library is MIT-licensed, not Apache-licensed, so Apache 2.0's file-marking condition was never applicable here.

items.rationale: Permissive licences make attribution travel with the code. MIT's whole condition is that the copyright notice and the permission notice be included in all copies or substantial portions of the software, and stripping them breaks that condition regardless of any other licence's separate rules.

items.stem: A supervisory authority finds that an organisation's processing violated GDPR's basic principles and imposes a temporary ban on that processing rather than issuing the maximum available fine. Why might the ban be the costlier consequence?

options.text: Because Article 58's corrective powers include imposing a temporary or definitive limitation, including a ban, on processing, which can stop the business operating in a way no fine amount does.
options.why: A processing ban can halt operations outright, which no fine, however large, does on its own.

options.text: It cannot be costlier; the fine is always the largest consequence a supervisory authority is able to impose.
options.why: The fine is the memorable consequence but not necessarily the costliest, because a processing ban can halt operations outright.

options.text: Because the upper fine tier under Article 83 reaches 20 million euros or 4 percent of worldwide annual turnover, whichever of the two figures happens to be lower.
options.why: Article 83's tiers apply whichever figure is higher, not lower, and this option also just restates the fine mechanism rather than explaining why a ban can cost more.

options.text: Because imposing a processing ban also starts HIPAA's 60-day individual-notification clock running.
options.why: HIPAA's 60-day clock governs breach notification to individuals under US law and has no bearing on a GDPR supervisory authority's processing ban.

items.rationale: GDPR Article 58 gives supervisory authorities corrective powers beyond fines, including imposing a temporary or definitive limitation, including a ban, on processing. Because that can stop a business operating altogether, it is often the costlier consequence even when the fine attached is comparatively modest.

items.stem: A breach at a card-accepting merchant results, from the same incident, in a regulator's fine, the loss of its card-acceptance agreement, a mandatory breach notification, and a visible drop in customer trust. What does this illustrate about the consequences of non-compliance?

options.text: That regulatory action, contractual loss, mandatory notification and reputational damage are distinct consequence types coming from different authorities, not interchangeable outcomes of one cause.
options.why: The four consequence types come from different authorities and are not interchangeable, which is exactly the point worth holding.

options.text: That the merchant is effectively being punished twice for the same offence, since one incident should only ever produce one consequence.
options.why: A single scenario can trigger all four named consequence types at once, each imposed by a different authority for a different reason.

options.text: That PCI-DSS, unlike GDPR, cannot impose more than one type of consequence for a single breach at the same time.
options.why: Nothing here limits how many consequence types a PCI-DSS-relevant breach can trigger; the card-acceptance loss is exactly a contractual consequence occurring alongside the others.

options.text: That the reputational damage will be reversed automatically once the fine is paid and the required notification has been sent.
options.why: Reputational damage lands last among the consequence types and is the one no remediation retracts, contradicting this option.

items.rationale: A single incident can trigger regulatory action, contractual loss, mandatory notification, and reputational or commercial damage all at once, because they come from different authorities acting on different grounds. None of the four substitutes for, or cancels out, any of the others.
